prompt.context: For many years, Jimmy Diners was a small successful chain of casual diners in the Boston metro area, operating primarily out of the suburbs. Two years ago, Jimmy Diners opened up four new locations in Boston/Cambridge near universities. The diners have been very successful, often with long lines of people waiting for tables. Unfortunately, these new restaurants have been less profitable than their suburban counterparts.
prompt.question: How would you approach solving this problem? What is driving the lower profitability of the urban diners, and how would you improve their performance?

clarifying_info.q: Is the quality of the two types of diners the same?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, quality of wait staff, food, etc. is the same.
Yes, the urban diners are in convenient locations.

clarifying_info.q: Are the basic non-food operating costs different between locations?
clarifying_info.a: No, rent, labor, SG&A, and utilities expenses are the same per store per month.

clarifying_info.q: Do both types of diners receive the same number of customers?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, urban and suburban diners receive the same number of customers and each customer buys the same number of menu items.

clarifying_info.q: How many customers does each type of diner receive per month?
clarifying_info.a: Both types of diners receive 4,000 customers per month.

clarifying_info.q: How many items does each customer order?
clarifying_info.a: Both suburban and urban customers order two items during each visit.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price per item?
clarifying_info.a: The price per item is $7.50 for suburban customers and $5.00 for urban customers.

clarifying_info.q: How long does each customer stay in the diner?
clarifying_info.a: Each customer stays on average for 100 minutes.

exhibits.title: Cost Table: Suburban vs. Urban Diners (per store per month)
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of monthly costs per diner for suburban vs. urban locations, broken down by cost category.
exhibits.data: Categories: COGS (food), Rent, Labor, SG&A, Utilities, Total

framework: Revenue drivers: number of customers, items ordered per customer, price per item
Cost drivers: variable costs (COGS/food), fixed costs (rent, labor, SG&A, utilities)
External/customer factors: customer profile differences (urban students vs. suburban adults), purchasing behavior, visit duration, timing

questions.prompt: Build a cost table comparing suburban and urban diners on a per-store, per-month basis. What does it reveal?
questions.guidance: Candidate should construct or accept the cost table and note that urban costs are actually LOWER than suburban costs. This is surprising given urban diners are less profitable, so revenue must be the culprit.

steps: Suburban: COGS $20,000 + Rent $8,000 + Labor $18,000 + SG&A $1,000 + Utilities $1,000 = $48,000
math.answer: Suburban total: $48,000/month; Urban total: $40,000/month. Urban costs are $8,000 LOWER than suburban.

questions.prompt: Now analyze revenues. What is the monthly revenue and profit for each type of diner?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate revenue using customers x items x price per item, then subtract costs to find profit. Key insight: urban revenue equals urban costs exactly, yielding zero profit.

math.setup: Monthly revenue = customers x items per customer x price per item; Profit = Revenue - Costs
steps: Suburban revenue: 4,000 customers x 2 items x $7.50 = $60,000
Urban revenue: 4,000 customers x 2 items x $5.00 = $40,000
math.answer: Suburban profit: $12,000/month. Urban profit: $0/month. Urban diners break even.

questions.prompt: Are fixed costs or variable costs contributing to low urban store profitability?
questions.guidance: The gross margin percentage is the same in both types of diners (COGS is proportional to revenue). Both have the same fixed cost base. Therefore urban diners need to increase volume (or price) to generate a contribution margin sufficient to cover fixed costs. The problem is revenue per customer, not cost structure per se.

steps: Fixed costs are identical at $28,000 for both
math.answer: Gross margins are similar; fixed cost base is identical. Urban diners need higher revenue per customer to generate profit.

questions.prompt: How would you improve the performance of the urban diners?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure ideas around two levers: (1) increase number of customers served (address wait times/throughput), and (2) increase revenue per customer (pricing, menu, bundling). Strong answers will link to the student/university customer profile.

math.setup: Kitchen efficiency improvement: current average stay = 100 minutes; 10% faster kitchen saves 10 minutes per customer
steps: 10% reduction in 100 minutes = 10 minutes saved per customer
10 minutes saved is modest and alone insufficient to close the profitability gap
math.answer: Saving 10 minutes per customer improves throughput but is insufficient on its own; must combine with other measures.

brainstorming.prompt: How would you improve the performance of the urban diners?

categories.name: Increase customer throughput
ideas: Improve kitchen efficiency using new techniques (10% faster)
Change ambience to encourage faster eating (e.g., faster background music)
Optimize table turnover and seating arrangements

categories.name: Increase revenue per customer
ideas: Raise menu prices for urban locations
Bundle items (combo meals) to increase average ticket
Unbundle items (e.g., sell fries separately from burgers) to increase total spend
Simplify menu to focus on higher-margin items

categories.name: Tailor to university/student customer base
ideas: Extend operating hours to stay open later into the night
Tailor menu items to student eating habits and preferences
Offer student pricing tiers or loyalty programs
Introduce late-night specials to capture incremental demand

categories.name: Operational improvements
ideas: Simplify menu to allow more advance prep work, improving kitchen speed
Cross-train staff for greater flexibility during peak hours

recommendation: Adopt new kitchen efficiency techniques to improve throughput and serve more customers per hour, reducing wait times.
Simplify the menu by eliminating low-demand and low-margin products; fewer SKUs enable advance prep and faster service.
Consider bundling or unbundling menu items strategically to increase revenue per customer visit.
Tailor the urban menu and hours to the student customer base (later hours, student-friendly options) to drive higher average spend.
risks: Menu simplification may reduce variety and deter some customers.
Pricing changes may be poorly received by price-sensitive student customers.
Ambience/atmosphere changes (e.g., faster music) could negatively affect the dining experience.
next_steps: Pilot kitchen efficiency techniques at one urban location and measure throughput improvement.
Conduct customer research on urban (student) preferences and willingness to pay.
Run a menu rationalization analysis to identify lowest-margin items for elimination.
Test bundled meal offers and track impact on average ticket size.
